title: Metals and Free Electron Theory
short_intro: Metals are crystalline solids characterized by high electrical and thermal conductivities arising from the presence of valence electrons moving freely through the periodic lattice of positive ions. The quantum mechanical treatment of these electrons overcomes the failures of the classical Drude-Lorentz model by incorporating Fermi-Dirac statistics and the Pauli exclusion principle.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Properties of metallic bonding, classical free electron theory (Drude model), Ohm's law derivation, electrical and thermal conductivity, Wiedemann-Franz law.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Quantum free electron theory (Sommerfeld model), Fermi-Dirac distribution function, Fermi energy, density of states, contact potential, thermionic emission, and band theory of solids.

prerequisites: Bohr's theory of hydrogen atom and quantum numbers

concept_notes.heading: Classical Free Electron Theory (Drude-Lorentz Model)
bullets: Treats valence electrons in a metal as an ideal gas of particles obeying classical Maxwell-Boltzmann statistics.
Assumes collisions with fixed positive ion cores are instantaneous and random, characterized by a mean free time between collisions.
Fails to explain the specific heat capacity of metals at room temperature and the temperature dependence of conductivity.

concept_notes.heading: Quantum Free Electron Theory (Sommerfeld Model)
bullets: Replaces classical statistics with Fermi-Dirac statistics, recognizing that electrons are fermions governed by Pauli's exclusion principle.
Electrons fill available energy states up to a maximum energy level at absolute zero, known as the Fermi energy (E<sub>F</sub>).
Successfully resolves the specific heat paradox by showing that only a small fraction of electrons near the Fermi surface participate in thermal excitation.

concept_notes.heading: Fermi-Dirac Distribution and Fermi Energy
bullets: The probability f(E) of an electron energy state being occupied at temperature T is given by the Fermi-Dirac function.
At absolute zero (T = 0 K), f(E) = 1 for E < E<sub>F</sub> and f(E) = 0 for E > E<sub>F</sub>.
At temperatures greater than 0 K, the distribution curve smears out around the Fermi energy within an energy range of roughly k<sub>B</sub>T.

concept_notes.heading: Density of States and Electrical Conduction
bullets: The density of states g(E) represents the number of allowed quantum states per unit volume per unit energy interval.
Electrical conduction occurs via the net drift of electrons near the Fermi level when an external electric field is applied.
The Wiedemann-Franz law relates thermal conductivity (&kappa;) and electrical conductivity (&sigma;) through the Lorenz number.

derivations.title: Drude Derivation of Electrical Conductivity
derivations.conditions: Uniform electric field E, constant relaxation time &tau;, classical electron gas
steps: Write the equation of motion for an electron of mass m and charge e in an electric field E: m(dv/dt) = -eE - m(v/&tau;).
Under steady-state conditions, the acceleration dv/dt = 0, yielding the drift velocity v<sub>d</sub> = (-e&tau;/m)E.
Express electric current density J as J = -nev<sub>d</sub>, where n is the electron concentration.
Substitute v<sub>d</sub> into J to get J = (ne<sup>2</sup>&tau;/m)E, and use Ohm's law J = &sigma;E to identify conductivity.

derivations.title: Fermi Energy at Absolute Zero
derivations.conditions: T = 0 K, free electrons in a three-dimensional box of volume V
steps: State the density of states for electrons including spin degeneracy factor 2: g(E)dE = \frac{V}{2\pi^2} \left(\frac{2m}{\hbar^2}\right)^{3/2} E^{1/2} dE.
Integrate the density of states from E = 0 to the Fermi energy E<sub>F</sub> to equate to the total number of electrons N: N = \int_{0}^{E_F} g(E)dE.
Rearrange the expression to solve explicitly for the Fermi energy E<sub>F</sub>.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Fermi-Dirac Distribution Function vs Energy
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Plot of f(E) on the y-axis against energy E on the x-axis, showing a step function at T = 0 K and a smeared curve with a pivot at E = E_F for T > 0 K.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates how thermal energy excites electrons across the Fermi level, allowing states slightly below E_F to be unoccupied and states above to be occupied.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in conceptual MCQs regarding occupation probability at and around the Fermi energy.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Density of States for 3D Free Electron Gas
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Parabolic curve of g(E) proportional to E<sup>1/2</sup> plotted against energy E.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that the number of available quantum energy states increases with the square root of energy in a three-dimensional metal.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in PGT derivations for total energy, number of electrons, and specific heat capacity.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Electrical Resistivity vs Temperature in Metals
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Linear increase of resistivity (&rho;) with temperature T at high temperatures, dropping to a residual resistivity at T &rarr; 0 K.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: At high temperatures, resistivity is proportional to phonon scattering (lattice vibrations); at low temperatures, impurity scattering dominates.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Contrasts classical predictions (&rho; &prop; T<sup>1/2</sup>) with quantum lattice vibration results (Gr&uuml;neisen formula).

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the relaxation time of conduction electrons in a metal having an electrical conductivity of 5.8 × 10<sup>7</sup> S/m, given that the free electron concentration is 8.5 × 10<sup>28</sup> m<sup>-3</sup> and mass of electron is 9.1 × 10<sup>-31</sup> kg.
solution_steps: Recall the formula for conductivity: &sigma; = ne<sup>2</sup>&tau; / m.
Rearrange to solve for relaxation time &tau;: &tau; = (&sigma; m) / (n e<sup>2</sup>).

solved_numericals.question: Find the Fermi energy of copper at 0 K, assuming each copper atom contributes one free electron. Given the density of copper = 8960 kg/m<sup>3</sup>, atomic weight = 63.5 g/mol, and Avogadro's number = 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>.
solution_steps: Calculate the electron concentration n = (Density × N<sub>A</sub>) / (Atomic Weight).
Use the Fermi energy formula: E<sub>F</sub> = (h<sup>2</sup> / 2m) × (3&pi;<sup>2</sup>n)<sup>2/3</sup>.
Substitute h = 6.626 × 10<sup>-34</sup> J s, m = 9.11 × 10<sup>-31</sup> kg to yield E<sub>F</sub> in Joules and convert to eV by dividing by 1.6 × 10<sup>-19</sup>.

solved_numericals.question: Determine the Fermi velocity of electrons in a metal having a Fermi energy of 5.5 eV. Take mass of electron as 9.1 × 10<sup>-31</sup> kg.
solution_steps: Convert Fermi energy from eV to Joules: E<sub>F</sub> = 5.5 × 1.6 × 10<sup>-19</sup> J = 8.8 × 10<sup>-19</sup> J.
Use the Fermi velocity relation: v<sub>F</sub> = \sqrt{2E_F / m}.
Calculate the final value: v<sub>F</sub> &approx; 1.39 × 10<sup>6</sup> m/s.

assumptions_and_limitations: The Sommerfeld model assumes a constant potential inside the metal (potential well approximation), ignoring the periodic potential of the ion cores which requires band theory for complete description.
Inter-electronic repulsion is neglected in the independent electron approximation, treated only in an averaged mean-field manner.

common_misconceptions.wrong: All free electrons in a metal contribute to the electronic specific heat at room temperature.
common_misconceptions.correct: Only a small fraction of electrons within an energy range of k_B·T of the Fermi surface are thermally excited.
common_misconceptions.why: Pauli's exclusion principle prevents electrons deeply seated in the Fermi sea from accepting thermal energy because nearby states are fully occupied.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The drift velocity of electrons is comparable to the speed of light or thermal velocity when current flows.
common_misconceptions.correct: Drift velocity is extremely small, typically on the order of millimeters per second.
common_misconceptions.why: Current is carried by the massive aggregate flow under an applied field, whereas the random thermal or Fermi velocity is immensely higher (~10^6 m/s).

quick_revision: Sommerfeld's quantum model replaces classical Maxwell-Boltzmann statistics with Fermi-Dirac statistics.
Fermi energy is the highest occupied energy level at absolute zero temperature.
Wiedemann-Franz law states that the ratio of thermal to electrical conductivity is directly proportional to temperature.
Drude conductivity is proportional to the square of the electronic charge and the relaxation time.
